text.p: Pianist David Helfgott, whose comeback from mental breakdown inspired the hit film "Shine," played Beethoven in his New York debut on Tuesday. He scored with a cheering audience but critics said Beethoven and music lost.

A sell-out crowd of more than 2,000 gave the Australian pianist five standing ovations and he literally jumped for joy on the stage of Avery Fisher Hall, muttering to himself, "Take a bow, take a bow."

New York, the sixth stop of Helfgott's 19-concert North American tour, followed a familiar pattern as the star ran on and off stage in a flowing white blouse with frilly cuffs and the audience and critics clashed in heated post-concert debates on the musical merits of his performance.

Simply put, U.S. critics, in review after review, detest Helfgott's playing and wonder publicly if the tour is really just a vehicle to exploit a mentally ill man and boost a film that is up for seven Academy Awards this month.

But concert-goers say the critics just don't get it. They spoke in interviews of coming to see a triumph of the human spirit and said it did not matter to them that Helfgott's interpretation of Beethoven's "Appassionata" sonata was to pound the keyboards and groan.

"What I am saying in my review ... is that he can play this music in the limited sense that he can push down the keys in the right order but it is totally disconnected from any sense of musicality. His hands remember how to play the notes but his phrasing is bizarre. He sounded and looked like a gifted but uninhibited child," New York News critic Terry Teachout said.

He said his review would be especially harsh because he wanted to bring audiences to their senses. In New York, as in earlier stops, Helfgott's show sold out to thousands of people paying up to $50 per ticket.
Many professional musicians at the concert were angry at the performance and violinist Isaac Stern departed at intermission, declining a New York Times reporter's request for comment.
In the film, Stern is shown inviting a then 14-year-old Helfgott to the United States as a prodigy, but the violinist said he did not remember such an incident.

Pianist Carol Aicher said, "His playing was very amateurish. There are conservatory students who can't get a chance to play in concert halls and yet he is here. This is all about money and marketing."
But lawyer Sidney Bernstein disagreed. "The audience is cheering for this man and for the human spirit. We know what he overcame and it was a wonderful experience just to hear him."
